title: A book a day until the holidays: how to make a simple book advent calendar
excerpt: Wrapping one book for each day of December has become a favourite family countdown. Here is how to set one up this weekend without buying 24 new books.

body.p: December starts on Tuesday, and many families are looking for a countdown that is calmer than a chocolate a day. One idea keeps growing in popularity: the book advent calendar. Instead of opening a little door, your child unwraps a book each evening and you read it together.

Publishers have noticed. This month Penguin Random House rounded up a whole range of ready-made book calendars, from 24 mini picture books in a box to seek-and-find collections, most priced around 30 US dollars. Publishers Weekly also reported on new countdown books with sealed pages or chapters that children open one day at a time. But you do not need to buy a boxed set to enjoy the tradition.

ul: Gather 24 books, or just 12 if that feels more manageable. A recent ThriftBooks guide suggests both options.
Mix old and new. Favourites from your own shelves, library books and second-hand finds all count. Children rarely mind seeing a well-loved story again.
Wrap each one in paper, newspaper or fabric and add a numbered tag.
Keep them in a basket or along a shelf where your child can see the numbers growing smaller.
Pick a set time, such as after dinner or at bedtime, so it becomes a ritual rather than a rush.

body.h: Make it work for your child

body.p: Variety keeps the countdown fun. Alternate cozy winter stories with funny books, a wordless picture book, a short non-fiction title about snow or animals, and an activity or sticker book for a busy weekend. If a younger sibling joins in, slip in a few sturdy board books. For a child who is starting to read alone, add one or two early readers they can try on their own, while you keep reading the longer picture books aloud.

The countdown does not have to be tied to one holiday. Families can simply count down to the winter break, a family visit or the last day of the year. What matters is the daily moment of opening something special and sharing it.

ul: Borrow most of the books from the library in late November and wrap them, then return them in January.
Swap a bag of books with another family so both children get new-to-them stories.
Leave the final days for one or two special new titles.

body.tip: Tonight, ask your child to help you choose five books from your shelves for the first days of December. Letting them pick, then forget, makes the unwrapping even more exciting.

title: Five everyday habits that strengthen your bond with your child
excerpt: Connection rarely needs grand gestures. A hug, a few minutes of undivided attention and a warm word can do more than you might think.

body.p: Between work, errands and screens, it is easy to feel that you do not spend enough quality time with your children. The good news is that closeness is built mostly from small, repeated moments rather than special outings.

ul: Greet your child with a hug or a warm word at the start of the day and when you are reunited after school.
Give a few minutes of full attention every day, phone away and body turned toward them.
Say what you appreciate about them, not only what they did well.
Keep a small ritual, such as a bedtime story or a goodnight chat, that your child can count on.
Repair after conflict: come back, apologize where needed and reconnect.

body.p: Children feel secure when they know the connection holds even on difficult days. Each of these habits tells them, without words, that they matter to you.

body.tip: Tonight, pick one moment (bath, car ride or bedtime) and give it your full attention for five minutes.

title: Get down to eye level: why it changes the conversation
excerpt: Kneeling or sitting down next to your child is a simple change that tells them they are heard, and it often makes hard conversations easier.

body.p: When an adult stands over a child to speak, the child may feel small or pressured. Lowering yourself to their height changes the feeling of the moment.

body.h: What changes when you lower yourself

ul: The child sees your face clearly, which helps them read your tone and expression.
The message feels like a conversation between equals rather than a lecture.
It is easier for a shy or upset child to open up and answer.
It is a visible signal that what they are saying matters to you.

body.p: This works for praise as well as for correction. A proud moment shared at eye level feels more personal, and a serious talk feels calmer.

body.tip: Next time you need to talk about something important, sit or kneel first, then speak slowly and make eye contact.

title: Listen first: ask what happened before you judge
excerpt: A simple question like 'What happened?' gives your child room to explain, and it often reveals more than the behavior you first noticed.

body.p: It is natural to react quickly when you see a problem: a spilled drink, a fight with a sibling, a broken rule. But the first version of events is not always the whole story.

body.h: How to listen before you correct

ul: Ask open questions such as 'What happened?' or 'Tell me more about that.'
Let your child finish without interrupting, even if you already think you know the answer.
Repeat back what you heard, for example: 'So you felt left out when your friend went ahead.'
Only then decide what to say about the behavior and what should happen next.

body.p: Children who feel heard are usually more willing to be honest, and that honesty is what makes guidance work. Listening does not mean agreeing with everything; it means understanding before you respond.

body.tip: At the next disagreement, ask one question and wait for the full answer before you say anything else.

title: Calm first: how to pause before you react to a child's behavior
excerpt: When frustration rises, a short pause and a slow breath can change how the next five minutes go, for you and for your child.

body.p: Every parent has had moments when a child's behavior triggers a strong reaction. Children learn how to handle big feelings partly by watching how the adults around them handle theirs.

ul: Notice the signs in your own body: a tight jaw, a raised voice, a fast heartbeat.
Take one slow breath, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath.
Name your feeling to yourself: 'I am frustrated right now.'
Then respond to the situation, not to the first urge.

body.p: A calm adult does not mean a permissive one. Boundaries still matter, but they land better when they are delivered in a steady voice. If you lose your temper, you can return later, apologize and explain what you were feeling.

body.tip: When you feel the urge to react fast, count to three and breathe out slowly before you speak.

title: Name the feeling, explain the rule, reassure the love
excerpt: Three steps help children understand big emotions and limits: put words to the feeling, explain the reason, and remind them they are loved.

body.p: Children often act out feelings they do not yet have words for. Helping them name what they feel is one of the most useful things a parent can do.

ul: Name the feeling: 'You are upset because the tower fell down.'
Explain the rule calmly and briefly: 'We do not throw blocks, because they can hurt someone.'
Reassure the love: 'I still love you, and we can build it again together.'

body.p: Drawing, talking about pictures or looking at storybooks together can help children practice naming feelings. Books in which characters have big emotions and recover from them are a natural starting point.

body.tip: After a hard moment, try saying: 'That was hard. I still love you. What can we do next time?'

title: Paper book or tablet? What a new study says about learning words at story time
excerpt: A UK study of 99 preschoolers found children learned new words about as well from a simple tablet storybook as from a paper one. The bigger difference was how grown-ups read.

body.p: Many families now own both shelves of picture books and a tablet loaded with e-books, and parents often wonder whether one is better for learning. A study from Lancaster University in the UK, published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology and reported this week, offers a reassuring answer, with a useful twist.

Laura Diprossimo and Kate Cain worked with 99 children aged 4 and 5 and their caregivers. Each pair shared two storybooks: one on paper and one on an iPad. The digital books were deliberately plain, with no narration, animations or games, so the only real difference was the screen itself. Afterwards, children were tested on new words from the stories and on how well they understood them.

ul: On average, children learned new words about equally well from paper and from the tablet.
Children who already had a bigger vocabulary picked up more new words in both formats.
Children with stronger attention and self-control skills understood the story slightly better on the tablet, while children with weaker skills in those areas did better with paper.
Caregivers pointed, explained and asked fewer questions when reading from the tablet.

body.p: That last finding may matter most at home. The extra pointing, gesturing and chatting adults do around a story is a big part of how children learn new words, and it seems to fade a little when a screen is involved.

The study tested only simple e-books, not the interactive apps with sounds and games that many children use. Word learning was checked just a few minutes after reading, and most families taking part had university-educated parents. So this is one helpful piece of evidence, not the final word.

body.h: What this means for your family

ul: Both formats can work. A tablet book on a long car journey is not a lost reading moment.
Whatever the format, the conversation is the magic. Pause to point at pictures and explain unusual words.
If your child is easily distracted, paper books may help them follow the story.
Choose plain e-books over ones packed with games and pop-ups when the goal is reading together.

body.tip: Tonight, pick one new word from the bedtime story, such as 'enormous' or 'shiver'. Point to it in the picture, act it out together, then try to use it again at breakfast tomorrow.

sources.title: PsyPost: Study suggests cognitive skills shape how young children learn new words from screen versus paper books
Journal of Experimental Child Psychology: Individual differences in word learning from print and digital shared book reading

title: Thankful read-alouds: gratitude picture books and a simple story-time ritual
excerpt: With Thanksgiving arriving tomorrow in the US, here are cheerful gratitude picture books for ages 1 to 8, plus easy questions that turn any story into a thankful moment.

body.p: Thanksgiving falls on Thursday in the United States, and library displays and bookshop tables are full of turkeys, harvest tables and thank-you stories. Wherever you live, this is a lovely week to borrow the idea behind the holiday: noticing the good things in our lives and saying so out loud. Picture books make that easy, because the characters do the noticing first.

body.h: Gratitude books for the littlest listeners

ul: Duck, Duck, Gobble! by J.D. Forester, illustrated by Lydia Nichols: a board book in which a duck and other farm animals turn a holiday table upside down. School Library Journal suggests it as a lap-sit read for toddlers.
Construction Site: A Thankful Night by Sherri Duskey Rinker, illustrated by Helen Morgan: a rhyming lift-the-flap book where the trucks say thank you for their work.
Thanksgiving Friends by Tammi Salzano, illustrated by Seb Braun: a touch-and-feel introduction to the holiday and to friendship.

It's Almost Time for... Thanksgiving! by Maisha Oso, illustrated by Tom Knight: a new 2026 title in which a family gets ready with a menu, a parade and loved ones, while a rhyme keeps landing on the wrong holiday. Kirkus praised its bouncy verse and busy, detail-filled pictures.
The Crayons Give Thanks by Drew Daywalt, illustrated by Oliver Jeffers: the famous box of crayons from The Day the Crayons Quit say what they are grateful for.
At Our Table by Patrick Hulse, illustrated by Madelyn Goodnight: a look at what the holiday means to many different families.
Our Table by Peter H. Reynolds: Violet looks for ways to bring her busy family back together around the table, a gentle story about connection.

body.h: Turn any story into a thankful moment

body.p: You do not need a special book to talk about gratitude. Scholastic's parent guide suggests open-ended questions while you read, and they work with almost any story. Try one or two per book rather than all at once:

ul: What do you think this character is thankful for?
Who was kind in this story? How did it make the others feel?
If you were in the book, who would you want to thank, and why?
What is one way our family could show thanks this week?

body.p: Younger children may answer with a single word, such as a toy, a pet or pancakes, and that is perfect. Older children can draw or dictate a short thank-you note to someone from their own life, inspired by the characters.

Talking about a character's feelings gives children words for their own. Linking a story to real people, like a grandparent, a teacher or a friend, also builds comprehension, because kids practise connecting what they read to their world.

body.tip: Tonight, put a small jar next to the bedtime books. After the story, each person names one thing they were thankful for today, and a grown-up writes it on a slip of paper for the jar. Read them all together at the end of the month.

sources.title: School Library Journal: Thankful for Books: 8 Board and Picture Books to Celebrate Thanksgiving
Kirkus Reviews: It's Almost Time for... Thanksgiving! by Maisha Oso

title: The 10 Best Illustrated Children's Books of 2026, picked by the NYT and New York Public Library
excerpt: The New York Times and the New York Public Library have chosen this year's ten most beautifully illustrated picture books. Here is the list, and what makes each one worth a look.

body.p: Every year, The New York Times and the New York Public Library name ten picture books whose art stands out from everything else published that year. The award has been running for more than seven decades, and the 2026 list was chosen by a children's librarian, Kelly-Ann Smith, and two picture-book creators, Julie Fogliano and Edel Rodriguez.
It is a list judged on illustration, so it is a great place to look if you want books your child will pore over again and again, even before they can read the words.

ul: While We're Here by Anne Wynter, illustrated by Micha Archer: cut-paper collage that keeps pace with the rhythm of the text.
Duel by Shawn Harris: playful, inkblot-style pictures painted in tempera and acrylic.
Ahab and the White Whale by Manuel Marsol (translated by Chloe Garcia Roberts): thick, textured paintings that show off the fun of paint itself.
Mariposa's Journey by Belen Medina, illustrated by Juana Martinez-Neal: a girl looking for a safe new home, told alongside the monarch butterfly migration.
Night Ride by Christopher Myers: a wordless night-time bike ride through New York, drawn like stained glass.
Bored by Felicita Sala: a funny, very familiar look at what boredom feels like.
Goldfinches by Mary Oliver, illustrated by Melissa Sweet: mixed-media art that feels like a nature walk and a bird-watcher's notebook.
Kiki & Me by Leo Timmers (translated by David Colmer): a horse tells the story of a friendship, in big painted spreads and comic panels.
Between by Anna Walker: soft, glowing pictures in just two colours, made with spray paint and pencil.
The Heart of Our Home by Janelle Washington: layered cut-paper scenes of family meals and everyday rituals.

body.h: How to use a list like this at home

ul: Pick one or two titles that match something your child already loves: bikes, birds, horses, family.
Ask your local library to reserve them. Award lists are popular, so a hold saves a trip.
Try a 'picture walk' first: turn the pages together and talk only about the pictures before you read the words.
Wordless books like Night Ride are perfect for pre-readers. Let your child tell you the story.

body.tip: Choose one illustration tonight and ask your child: 'What do you think happens just after this picture?' It builds imagination, vocabulary and storytelling in one question.

title: Do audiobooks count as reading? What new research tells parents
excerpt: Almost half of children now listen to audiobooks or podcasts. New UK research suggests listening can be a doorway into reading, not a shortcut around it.

body.p: Many parents wonder whether a story in headphones is 'real' reading. The latest research from the UK's National Literacy Trust offers a reassuring answer: for many children, listening is one of the ways into books, not a replacement for them.

The charity's 2026 audio report, based on a survey of more than 110,000 children and young people aged 8 to 18, found that almost half now listen to audiobooks, podcasts or both. More than a quarter said that listening makes them more interested in reading books, and around three in ten audiobook listeners said audio helps them enjoy stories when reading on the page feels hard.

Children also told researchers that listening helps them relax, feel happy and feel more confident. A separate report published in October 2026 looked at families with children under five and found that audio stories are already a normal part of everyday life for many of them, with parents pointing to benefits for language, learning and wellbeing.

ul: It builds vocabulary and background knowledge, which children later need to understand what they read.
It lets children enjoy stories that are above their current reading level.
It models expressive reading: pauses, voices and feeling.
It can be a lifeline for children who find decoding tiring or who have dyslexia.
Pair the audiobook with the printed book so your child can follow the words.
Use audio in 'dead time': car journeys, tidying up, waiting rooms.
Talk about the story afterwards, just as you would after a read-aloud.
Keep shared read-alouds too. Your voice and your lap are still the best format for little ones.

body.p: Researchers are clear that audio is not meant to replace learning to read. Children still need daily practice with print. But if a story in headphones gets a reluctant reader excited about books, that is a win.

body.tip: Next time your child finishes an audiobook, borrow the paper version and let them find their favourite scene in the book. It turns listening into reading in a natural way.

title: Reading together is back: why schools are turning to shared reading
excerpt: As fewer children read for pleasure, teachers are bringing back an old idea: reading the same book together, out loud and in class. Here is what it looks like, and how to do it at home.

body.p: Teachers in many countries report the same worry: fewer children choose to read for fun, and it is getting harder to keep them engaged with books at school and at home. A new report from Education Week in October 2026 looked at what schools are doing about it, and one idea stands out: reading together.

In one sixth-grade classroom in Georgia, featured in the report, students now do most of their reading as a group, in class. The aims are simple: build fluency, create a shared buzz around the book, and make sure every child actually reaches the last page. The report's wider message is that a mix of adults modelling reading, teacher guidance, small rewards and family involvement works better than any single trick.

Schools are also reaching out to families. The report describes community reading nights where parents and young children read side by side, and school librarians who work with teachers to build a reading culture from the very first years of school.

This fits with UK findings from the National Literacy Trust in 2026: reading enjoyment ticked up for the first time in five years, but remains low, and children are much more likely to read regularly when reading is linked to their interests and supported by the people around them.

ul: Pick one 'family book' and read a chapter or a few pages together every evening.
Take turns: you read a page, your child reads a line or a speech bubble.
Stop at an exciting moment and guess what happens next.
Let siblings join in: older children can read to younger ones.
Celebrate finishing: a special snack, a drawing of the ending, or choosing the next book.

body.tip: Shared reading does not have to be long. Ten minutes of reading the same story together, at the same time each day, does more for the habit than one long session at the weekend.

title: Afraid of the dark? Gentle ways to help little ones with bedtime fears
excerpt: Most children go through a phase of night-time fears. Here is why it happens, and calm, simple ways to help your child feel safe at bedtime.

body.p: If your little one suddenly needs the hall light on, checks under the bed or calls you back three times after lights out, you are far from alone. Paediatric sleep teams describe night-time fears as a normal part of growing up: most children have them at some point, and fear of the dark is one of the most common.

Children's Hospital Colorado notes that nearly three in four children aged 4 to 12 report night-time fears. They tend to appear as children's imaginations grow and they begin to understand that things can go wrong, while young children still find it hard to separate what is real from what is imagined.

ul: Talk about the fear in daylight, when everyone is calm, rather than at the tense moment of lights out.
Take the fear seriously. Don't tease, even gently, and don't try to argue it away.
Keep the bedtime routine predictable: bath, pyjamas, story, cuddle, lights out, in the same order every night.
Offer small tools for control: a soft night light, a favourite cuddly toy, or a torch they can switch on themselves.
Practise brave thoughts together, such as 'The dark is just my room with the lights off.'
Read stories about characters who feel scared and discover they are safe after all.
Show quiet confidence that your child can handle it. Children borrow our calm.

body.p: Most children grow out of these fears over a few weeks or months. If fears are severe, last a long time or affect daytime life, it is worth talking to your child's doctor.

body.tip: Before bed tonight, walk around the darkened room together with a torch and name everything you find: the chair, the books, the teddy. Familiar shapes turn the dark back into home.

title: Mazes, colouring and crayons: why activity books are more than busywork
excerpt: A quiet afternoon with crayons and a maze builds more than you might think: the hand control, focus and planning children later need for writing and reading.

body.p: Activity books can look like a simple way to keep little hands busy. But child development experts see colouring, tracing and mazes as real practice for skills that matter at school.

The first is fine motor control, the small movements of the wrist and fingers. Scholastic's parenting team points out that the preschool years are an especially important time for these skills, which children also use to button a coat or hold a spoon. When a child starts colouring inside the lines, it is a sign that both motor and thinking skills are developing.

Mazes add something extra. To solve one, a child has to stop, look ahead, choose a path and correct course, which exercises attention and planning. Occupational therapists often cite research in the journal Child Development (Cameron and colleagues, 2012) showing that fine motor skills and executive function each contribute to how children do in kindergarten.

body.h: Getting the most from activity pages

ul: Choose pages with big, simple shapes and thick lines for younger children; add detail as they grow.
Offer chunky crayons first, then pencils as grip improves.
Let them choose the colours. Purple grass is perfectly fine.
Sit alongside and do a page yourself. It becomes time together, not a chore.
Stop while it is still fun. Five calm minutes beat twenty frustrated ones.
Link pages to a story you just read, so the activity becomes a way to retell it.

body.tip: After tonight's story, ask your child to draw their favourite moment from it, then tell you about the picture. Drawing, talking and remembering, all in one.

title: Sounds and words: the two early skills that best predict reading success
excerpt: A large research review highlighted this month finds that hearing the sounds inside words and knowing lots of words matter most for reading. The good news: both grow through everyday play and talk.

body.p: If your child is slow to start reading, it is easy to worry that something is wrong. New research shared this month by Texas A&M University offers a calmer and more useful way to look at it.

A team led by educational psychologist Daniel Hajovsky combined about 50,000 correlations from 137 different cognitive and achievement tests into a single statistical model. The goal was to see which thinking skills are most closely linked to reading. Two stood out above everything else: auditory processing, meaning the ability to notice and tell apart the sounds in words, and comprehension-knowledge, meaning vocabulary and general background knowledge.

Visual processing showed no meaningful link with reading ability in the model. General intelligence did play a part, but a smaller one than some earlier reviews suggested. Memory, reasoning and processing speed acted more as supporting players. As Hajovsky put it, "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability."

This is a research review, not a classroom trial, so it describes links rather than proving cause and effect. Still, it fits with what reading teachers have long seen: children who can play with sounds and who know many words tend to find reading easier.

Concern about early literacy is in the news. A Canadian report covered by Regina's 620 CKRM this week said roughly one in three Canadian children cannot read proficiently by Grade 4. Libraries there are answering with storytimes, rhyme programmes and book bags for new parents, all aimed at building exactly these early skills.

body.h: Easy ways to build both skills at home

ul: Rhyme together. Nursery rhymes, silly songs and rhyming picture books train the ear to hear sound patterns.
Play I Spy with sounds: I spy something that starts with mmm. Mug! Moon! Mum!
Clap the beats in names and words: but-ter-fly has three claps.
Talk about the pictures during story time. Ask what is happening and introduce one new word, like enormous or soggy.
Read nonfiction too. Books about trucks, oceans or the human body build the background knowledge that helps later understanding.
Narrate everyday life. Cooking, shopping and walks are full of new words and ideas to chat about.

body.p: For children aged 3 to 5, keep it playful and short. For 6 to 8 year olds who are reading on their own, keep up the conversation: ask them to explain a word or tell you what they learned. If a child still struggles despite practice, talk with their teacher. Targeted help for a specific skill usually works better than more of the same.

body.tip: Tonight at bedtime, pick a rhyming book and pause before the last word of each rhyme. Let your child guess it from the sound.

sources.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

title: Why reading to a dog helps shy readers (and how to try it at home)
excerpt: Libraries are inviting children to read aloud to calm therapy dogs, and research suggests the gentle audience can lift confidence. Here's how to borrow the idea at home, with or without a pet.

body.p: Last week a Florida library system made local news for a simple idea: children reading picture books aloud to a dog. The Alachua County Library District runs a Read With a Dog programme in which elementary-aged children sit beside a certified therapy dog and read to it. Librarians and parents told WUFT News they have seen children grow more confident.

Why a dog? A dog never corrects a mispronounced word, never sighs and never looks at the clock. For a child who is still sounding out words, that patient, non-judging listener can take the pressure off.

The evidence is encouraging but still small. A 2022 study in the Early Childhood Education Journal followed 24 Canadian children aged about 7 to 8 who needed extra reading support. Each child spent eight weeks reading to a dog and eight weeks reading to an adult, about 15 minutes a week. Oral reading and comprehension improved in both programmes, so the dog was not magic. But the children were noticeably more enthusiastic about the dog sessions, and only the dog sessions were described as calm. Parents and teachers saw better attitudes to reading after both.

An earlier UC Davis project found similar gains in reading fluency among children who read to rescue dogs each week. Even so, researchers are careful: a reading dog builds comfort and motivation, while skills still come from teaching and practice.

body.h: How to bring the idea home

ul: Ask your local library whether it hosts a reading-dog session.
If you have a calm family pet, invite your child to read a short book to it. Five to ten minutes is plenty.
No pet? A favourite stuffed animal works too. Let your child be the teacher who shows the pictures and reads the story.
Choose easy, familiar books for these sessions. The goal is fluency and fun, not a challenge.
Stay nearby but quiet. Resist correcting every slip; praise the effort afterwards.
Younger children (3 to 5) can 'read' by retelling a story from the pictures. That counts too.

body.tip: Tonight, set out a cushion, a teddy or the family dog, and a book your child already knows well. Ask: Can you read this one to Teddy? Then just listen.

title: Cozy picture books are topping the 2026 holiday gift lists
excerpt: The season's gift guides are full of warm, funny picture books. Here's what's getting attention, and a simple way to pick the right book for the child on your list.

body.p: Gift-guide season has arrived, and this year the children's lists lean cozy. The Associated Press holiday roundup mixes snug board books with a few delightfully spooky reads, and one title that keeps coming up is Your Truck by Jon Klassen, published by Candlewick Press. Klassen's dry humour and quiet pictures have made him a favourite with parents who read the same book forty nights in a row.

November also brought a strong crop of new releases. Book Riot's monthly roundup highlights Good Bear, Bad Bear by Hyewon Yum, out November 3: a little girl decides that if her sister is always the good one, she must be the bad one. It is a gentle doorway into a feeling many siblings know well. And for early readers who love comics, the newest Dog Man by Dav Pilkey is the most anticipated children's book of the month.

Award season is underway too. The New York Times and New York Public Library have named their ten Best Illustrated Children's Books of 2026, a list worth browsing if you want a book that will also look beautiful on the shelf.

body.h: How to choose a picture book gift

ul: Ages 0–2: sturdy board books with bold pictures, rhythm and repetition.
Ages 3–5: a story with a clear feeling at its heart (fear of the dark, a new sibling, sharing) and pictures that reward a second look.
Ages 6–8: longer read-alouds, funny early chapter books and comics that build confidence.
Any age: think about what the child already loves (trucks, animals, space) and start there.

body.tip: Write a short message on the first page before you wrap it. A dated inscription turns a book into a keepsake a child will find again years later.

title: Learning to read vs. choosing to read: why the bedtime story still matters
excerpt: A 2026 publishing report warns that a heavy focus on literacy skills can crowd out the joy of reading. A calm bedtime routine is one of the easiest fixes.

body.p: Every year, HarperCollins Children's Books and Farshore publish a review of children's reading for pleasure. The 2026 edition, built on NielsenIQ data and research with The Reading Agency, carries a pointed theme: there is a difference between a child who can read and a child who chooses to.

The report's argument is that literacy can be taught and tested, while the love of reading has to be encouraged, modelled and kept free of pressure. When reading at home starts to feel like more homework, some children quietly stop picking up books on their own. Its practical answer is a regular reading routine: a predictable, relaxed moment with a book that children come to look forward to.

That matters because shared reading has been slipping. An Education Week report in 2025 found that only about a third of parents of five- to seven-year-olds said they regularly read to their children.

body.h: Five ways to make bedtime reading feel like a treat

ul: Let your child choose the book, even if it's the same one every night.
Keep it short. Ten unhurried minutes beat a rushed half hour.
Do the voices. Children remember the silly ones for years.
Talk about the pictures and ask what they think happens next.
Never use reading as a punishment or a chore to tick off.

body.tip: Dim the lights, put the phones in another room and end with the same closing words each night. The ritual itself tells a child's body it is time to rest.

title: Kids' reading for fun is rising again. Here's how to keep it going at home
excerpt: After a 20-year low, children's enjoyment of reading has ticked up for the first time in five years. But young boys are moving the other way.

body.p: There is some good news for families who love books. The National Literacy Trust's 2026 Annual Literacy Survey, answered by more than 125,000 children and young people across the UK aged 5 to 18, found that reading enjoyment and daily reading have risen for the first time in five years, after hitting a 20-year low in 2025.

The lift is modest. Just over one in three children aged 8 to 18 (36.1%) said they enjoyed reading. Among the youngest readers, aged 5 to 8, enjoyment is still high at 61.6%, but it slipped slightly from the year before, and the drop came from boys. The survey also found the gap between children from lower-income families and their peers is widening.
The Trust's main lesson is simple: children read more in their free time when books connect to what they already care about.

ul: Follow their interests: dinosaurs, football, space, animals. Any topic is a way in.
Count everything: comics, joke books, recipes and magazines are all real reading.
Keep books within reach, in the car, by the bed, next to the sofa.
Let them see you reading. Children copy what we do far more than what we say.
For boys aged 5 to 8 especially, try funny books, comics and stories full of action.

body.tip: Visit the library together once a month and let your child choose freely. Owning the choice is half the fun.
